newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: More falls on horizon for Irish pound - economists.
newsitem.headline: More falls on horizon for Irish pound - economists.

text.p: The beleaguered Irish pound slipped quietly into a holiday weekend licking its wounds late on Friday after a week of turmoil but further falls in the currency are still on the cards, economists said.

"The odds are the punt will come under further selling pressure when the markets re-open on Tuesday," Riada economist Padhraic Garvey told Reuters. "There have been bigger fish to fry this end of the week with Britain's election and Europe's holiday and now Ireland and Britain's May holiday on Monday."

In a week of exceptional turbulence the punt suffered a severe sell-off plunging four percent against the mark on Wednesday and Thursday and plummeting three percent against sterling, hitting a five-year low against the British currency.
The currency's plunge was triggered by indications from Ireland's central bank late on Tuesday that it was not going to intervene to shore up the ailing currency.
The central bank had been intervening heavily to support the Irish unit until then.

Speculators took this as a signal that the Irish authorities were going to let the currency drop closer to the median rate within the European Exchange Rate Mechanism in anticipation of entry into a single currency in 1999. This meant a drop to 2.41 marks.

The Irish pound, which closed at 2.6649 marks and 0.9499 stg on Monday, dipped to lows of 0.91 stg and 2.5530 marks mid-week. By the close of business on Friday it steadied to 2.5768/83 marks and 0.9240/70 stg.
"Ultimately I expect it to fall to 2.55 marks and 91 sterling next week," said Jim Power, economist with Bank of Ireland Group Treasury.

A surprise 50 basis point interest rate rise by Ireland's central bank on Thursday and sterling's fall after a landslide victory for Britain's Labour Party on Friday combined to ease the pressure temporarily on the Irish currency.
Sterling shed around three pfennigs in early trade on Friday as dealers took profits and trimmed long positions in the wake of the Labour Party's sweeping victory in the British elections.
Later in the day the British unit regained some of its losses shrugging of its post-election jitters.
Meanwhile Ireland's central bank intervened to reduce interbank rates on Friday morning.

"Central bank intervention had a very positive impact this morning and on the day short yields are down and that reflects the fact that the central bank was in pumping liquidity back into the market," one dealer said.
Key one month interbank rates were pushed down to 6.31/43 percent late on Friday having peaked at 6.75/7.25 percent in the height of the punt sell-off.
Bank of Ireland's Jim Power said a lot of money had been made over the week and the punt could run into short-covering profit-taking when it re-opened on Tuesday.
"That could be enough to get the punt to approach 2.60 marks but then I would expect it to run into serious selling pressure."
